utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please, and good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Same advisory to the accused, that at any time you're not receiving interpretation, please draw our attention straight away. I see just one change in the Nikolic team. Mr. Nicholls is here as well, okay. So any preliminaries? Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all I'd like to tell you that Mr. Petrusic is now with the Defence team of General Miletic as a legal adviser. This is the first thing. Second thing, it is somewhat embarrassing for the Defence, it has to do with the next witness, Mr. Ruez. Indeed, we realised that we had not received all the testimony or the previous statements made earlier on by Mr. Ruez. He testified in four cases, Krstic, Blagojevic, Erdemovic, and Mladic and Karadzic. Further to Rule 61 proceedings. We received the Krstic and Blagojevic testimony transcripts but we did not for Karadzic and Mladic. We also did not receive his testimony in the Erdemovic case in B/C/S. We got it in English but in the in B/C/S. He's a rather important witness. And it is somewhat embarrassing as I said because the Defence would not like to ask for the proceedings to be stayed, but on the other land, it seems difficult to start his testimony before the accused were able to read his previous testimony transcripts in a language that they understand, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's my understanding the testimony from Erdemovic that Ms. Fauveau speaks of, they've had for I think over a year or two, so we are getting that audio as soon as possible, though, but that is something that I think both sides missed. The Rule 61 hearing, we -- several people testified briefly at that and we caught everyone but somehow Mr. Ruez slipped through the cracks. That was public testimony that he did in 1996 before any of us were here and Ms. Fauveau is absolutely right and she did find that in the record, the public record. And we have been able to give that to her in English and we are getting that B/C/S audio recording as soon as possible. I hope to have CDs today to give to people so that over the next week or so, while Mr. Ruez is testifying, that they will be able to review that. It's relatively short, and it's Mr. Ruez speculating about things, but it is important that they have it and we will get them to them as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. I think the position is easy enough to handle. First of all I wish to apologise to you, Mr. Petrusic but this column has stood in the way so I couldn't see you. And welcome to this Tribunal, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the other side. There is just one correction for the transcript though, my name is Nenad Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Fauveau, that being said, are you withdrawing your motion appealing against the registrar's decision?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, because Mr. Petrusic is a legal adviser. He has been a legal adviser for a year but he's not a co-counsel. As a result, he cannot perform all the duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. I just wanted to clarify that. The other thing is this: Basically, if we adhere to the time schedule that has been indicated by the Prosecution for witness Ruez, and also that indicated by each one of you, we are basically talking of another two weeks before your turn comes up. So by which time I suppose this shortcoming would have been addressed and remedied. If as we go along, you see that it's not, then please draw our attention immediately and we will take action. On the other hand, I can't emphasise enough, Mr. McCloskey, that you attend to this, the sooner the better, because otherwise I would -- I would obviously then have to accept that there is a problem which would require some kind of remedy on our part. So all right, for the time being I think we can leave it at that. I think we can bring the witness in, if there are no further matters to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, I'm sure the Defence knows I was joking when I said Mr. Ruez was speculating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They take you very seriously, actually. Incidentally I barely need to repeat what I stated yesterday, that today we are still sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis(A). All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I welcome you again to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We had a long session yesterday. Today, please God, it will be shorter. It will be shorter. And I suppose that within the next hour or so, you would be able to enjoy the brief break that you asked for before you return back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It will be as you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I just wanted to remind you that yesterday you made a solemn declaration before us that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and I just wanted to confirm to you that you don't need to repeat it again today because it still holds good.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It holds for as long as I'm in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I thank you. I'm going to hand you to Mr. Kergvic -- no, Mr. Stojanovic, Mr. Stojanovic, who is appearing for accused Borovcanin, and hopefully he will conclude his cross-examination within the next ten minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hasic.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In order to continue I just wanted to remind you briefly with a sentence where we broke off yesterday with our cross-examination. If you remember, you said that you had passed the first check-point in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That about 150 to 200 people were being let through there.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That men were being -- men, women, and children were being allowed to pass there.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then some 15 metres farther, there was another check-point where men were separated from the women and children.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were separated from your family at that second check-point?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the second one, and I was turned into the house, told to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And there you were told that you are going to be interrogated, after which you would be transferred to Tuzla; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but some women were crying, they didn't want the men to go. They said, no, it will be just a short interrogation and then they will be sent to Tuzla, but obviously this didn't happen. They would always say one thing and do something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who told you that? Did anyone tell you that personally?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from the soldiers who were directing us where to go, just a brief interrogation, it's going to be, and then you're going to go to Tuzla. This is what a Serbian soldier was telling the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After spending an hour or two at that house, you were transferred to the elementary school in Bratunac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Vuk Karadzic school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You left your food bag at the entrance to the school?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the bags with food and whatever else people had in their bags.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember if you had your identification documents with you, your ID card?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't. It was left in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any identification documents with you?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Some of the things like that were left at home in the village. When you're fleeing you don't think of anything else other than saving your life. When you flee everything else is left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And that house in Potocari, was food taken away from anyone, ID, bags?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not there. There they were proceeding quite nicely, until the separation took place. When the separation happened, as soon as we came to Bratunac, it was completely different. They were angry. That's when the killing started, the beatings, people being taken out. All of these things started happening then, as soon as we arrived to the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, there was no mistreatment at the house in Potocari. It started happening in Bratunac only?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see anything like that at the house. There was just that one man who was looking, who was requesting money and this one man who gave it to him. There was no harassment there. There was no separation. Soldiers were outside. They were not inside with us. The soldiers were outside separating people but they were not inside with us to interrogate us or to mistreat us. They had different tasks to perform. They were not sitting inside with us so they didn't mistreat us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And at the end, just one more question, Mr. Hasic. You spoke about that yesterday in response to questions by Their Honours. You described this policeman who entered the Bratunac school. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: He was wearing a blue police uniform?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue uniform, white belt, white holster, a gun, white gun holster. I cannot say what kind of a policeman he is, whether he was a military or a civilian policeman. It's not clear to me what he was. He was a member of some kind of police, though, because he had this belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I want to ask you about, that blue uniform of his. Was it multi-coloured or was it of one colour?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a uniform of just one colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Stojanovic. Madam Fauveau? Madam Fauveau will be cross-examining you. And she is appearing for General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a few questions for you with regard to what you experienced in Potocari and Bratunac. When you were in Potocari, you did not see personally any murders, is this right?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see, but I did hear people outside screaming, the people that were taken outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, and when you were in Bratunac, you did not witness any murders either, personally, right?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were separated from your family in Potocari, in the house where you were taken to, you didn't see anything wrong there, is this right?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can it be said that on the 11th of July you left Srebrenica before the Serbs entered the city?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left earlier. Had I waited there, I wouldn't have left the town at all. My bones would have been there still.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, is there anything wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so the answer of the witness is not recorded in the transcript because here it's page 8, line 16. There were two questions posed by Mrs. Fauveau and first was when you were separated from your family in Potocari in the house where you were taken to, you didn't anything wrong there; is that right? And then after that, the witness answered, yes. And his answer was not recorded. So can it be said is the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So, Mr. Hasic, you've heard Mr. Lazarevic's intervention. You were asked by Madam Fauveau --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- whether you saw anything wrong in Potocari when you were separated from your family.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that house. I didn't see anything, as far as the house is concerned. But I heard from others that that they were taking some people outside, behind the house, but this is something that I heard from others. I didn't see it. For as long as I was in the house, no one was beating anyone, no one was mistreating people. So as far as the house is concerned, it was all right. After an hour and a half or two we were transferred to Bratunac and this is where they started. We left our bags there and then they started to beat us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, is it right to say that the UNPROFOR organised the evacuation of the people from Srebrenica in Potocari on the 11th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who organised that. I know that there were two buses. We got into the buses. It was probably organised by the Serb army. The buses and then to Bratunac, because the UNPROFOR was -- they had their hands tied at the time. They were not free to do what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, when you left Srebrenica to go to Potocari, the Serbian army was not present in Srebrenica, is this right?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, in the Petric area of town, there were bullets flying constantly and then also there was constant shelling, shells were falling in the town and around the town as well. No one asked whether there were women there, children, who was there. They were shelling the town. They were shelling civilians. This was ethnic cleansing. We all know this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, did UNPROFOR evacuate you from Srebrenica to Potocari on the 11th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As long as the UNPROFOR was just below the hospital, they brought out the wounded, they placed them on the trucks. I remember there were two trucks with the wounded. The UNPROFOR people were there and the trucks were moving slowly. They couldn't move fast because of the people. It was a very long column that went to Potocari. The column perhaps had already arrived at Potocari but there were people still in Srebrenica that were part of the column. The road was full of people. It wasn't a column where you would have one person walking behind another. The whole road was full of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you left Srebrenica on that day, on the 11th of July 1995, in order to go to Potocari, you did not intend to stay in Potocari forever, is this right?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my intention to stay there. Why would I stay in Potocari? If I had wanted to stay I would have stayed in Srebrenica in my house. I would have stayed there. Why would I stay in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Intended to go to Tuzla, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have the intention but it was by force. I had to go. Had I not gone, I would be in a mass grave in Potocari now and they did find two mass graves there. It was better to leave, to save my life when I could. If not, then that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You intended to go as early as the 12th of July, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did intend to go had they wanted to take me. But they didn't want to take me so you had to wait and see where you would be taken to, whether to a place where you would perish or somewhere where you could survive. They were telling us one thing and doing another.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it not right to say that on the 12th of July 1995, in Potocari, you could not make it to the buses because you didn't want to have to push and shove in the crowd?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very crowded, and I didn't see any atrocities that first night so I wasn't in a hurry and it was very crowded. The second night, when I saw the atrocities, what was being done, how things were being done, then the next day, this was a Thursday, there was a very big crowd. You couldn't really go through. I was travelling maybe from the morning until the afternoon, until 2.00 in the afternoon, and I covered perhaps just 100 metres, until I reached this check-point where I was supposed to be to go through, to pass. So many people were all trying to get there. Many people fainted because of the heat, because of the crowd. There were fainting, then the UNPROFOR people were taking them away or they were being taken to the UNPROFOR so they could get first aid, something being taken to the UNPROFOR so they could get first aid, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can it be said that even on the 13th of July nobody forced you to go to the check-point?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military did. As long as their shells were falling, that meant that whoever remained there didn't survive. That needs to be made clear, be it a child, a woman, a man, regardless. There were some people who were infirm, who were ill. They were unable to move. They never went anywhere. Why do you think there are so many mass graves everywhere, if all those people weren't killed? You're trying something --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it right to say that in the day, on the 12th of July, Serbs took bread to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Also took water there?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They brought water to the people there, and they would throw food to the people, if that's what you're asking. As for water, people would bring water for themselves. They would go and fetch it in bottles, containers, whatever they had. This was while I was in Potocari, while I was there, within the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, is it not right to say that you still had food with you when you got to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. If he's already stated that when he arrived in Bratunac they took his food away, why are you asking the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you went to Bratunac with the food, did your family in Potocari still have some food with them?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, are you sure that you had to leave your food before you entered the school in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely, 100 per cent so, because if somebody ordered you to do something you had to do it. If you failed to do it, they would hit you with a rifle butt on your back, so you would have to keep quiet.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You testified before this Tribunal in the Blagojevic case on the 14th of July 2003, page 1182 and you said this: [In English] "And there we got to the school Vuk Karadzic. That is the name of the school. When we got to the school, we all had to leave our bags if we had any and take the food with us." [Interpretation] Is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. The food remained there and the bags. Where was I supposed to put the food? Was I supposed to put it in my pockets? No. It remained there in the bags. They made us leave the bags. That is to say they didn't give us our food to eat. They didn't bring us any food, because they wanted us to die of hunger so that when they were leading people away, we would be subdued, our hands were tied on our backs and they were armed. We were totally subdued, unable to provide any resistance. This lasted for three or four days. We had no food at all. We were half dead by then.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell me who told you that the school where you were in Bratunac was the Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Others who knew what the school was called told me that, the people who had attended that school, who went to that school, the students of that school. They used to be the students at that school. It's an old school now and it's been abandoned. They built a new school now because in this old school, they had prisoners there. I asked other people what the school was called and the people who knew that told me, Vuk Karadzic. And there is an elementary school there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Hasic and Madam Fauveau, what's more important is the time that you came to know that that was indeed the Vuk Karadzic school. Was it at the same time you were being detained there, that you got there, or was it later on that you came to know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know it then. I found that out subsequently. I said I was in that school and I don't know what it's called, and people then told me that the school was called Vuk Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, when you were in the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac, in the room where you were, were there people you knew?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people. There were my people there, Muslims. As for Serbs, they were the army, and I didn't know them. I'm telling you as it is. I can't tell you I knew that soldier or this soldier. I didn't. I didn't know any of them. Only one of them told me that he was from the village called Gnjena. This was the policeman who beat this man. Then the soldier from Gnjena fetched a hose so that the policeman could beat this man with a hose. And I knew that he was from Gnjena because at one point he asked, "Do you know anybody who lived in my house in Gnjena?" This is how I originally learned that he was from the village of Gnjena.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Among the Muslims who were with you in that room, was there anybody you knew?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about two of them, I think. They were sort of my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, your neighbours were in your hometown or in Srebrenica? Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the place where I come from, they were from neighbouring villages. I recognised these two men and I knew them. Not that I just recognised them. I knew them from before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So you're using the word "neighbours" in the sense that they came from neighbouring villages, not in the sense that they lived next door to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, neighbouring villages, other villages, but our villages are small, they are not large. Perhaps there are 20 to 30 houses in any given village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Madam Fauveau. And my apologies to you for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were in the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac, your brothers were not with you, were they?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any there. As for Pilica, I saw one.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm only talking about Bratunac. I'm only talking about Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any of them there, not in that room. Perhaps they were in some other rooms, because people were leaving Potocari and going on for four or five days. They were travelling on that road going through Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At any rate, you cannot say with any certainty that one of your brothers was killed in Bratunac, is this right?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say, because they were found in Pilica, in mass graves there. Last year, I buried one of them on the 11th of July, and the second one I buried this year on the 11th of July. They were both found in Pilica. Both of them were older than me. One was by five years older and the other one seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: -- were killed. Sir, excuse me, I do not deny the fact that they were killed. What I'm asking you is whether you knew whether they were killed in Bratunac or not.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: It was asked and answered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say that they were killed in Bratunac when they were found in a mass grave in Pilica. It means that they were killed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, let me come back to Potocari. Yesterday, transcript page 7, you stated that you spent the first night outside in Potocari. Is this right?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You also testified that you had been separated from your family. You had lost them that first night, is this right?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I got separated from them. I thought that they were outside. And I didn't find them until the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 20th of March 1996, you made a statement. Can it be shown to the witness? It is Exhibit 7 -- 712. Page 1 of the statement, first paragraph, second sentence, you stated this:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you please make sure the witness is able to see this? You can see from here. Okay. Thank you. Yes. Go ahead, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It is the second sentence in the first paragraph. This is what you stated: [In English] "My family and other civilians, I spent the night in Potocari in the factory buildings." [Interpretation] Do you remember making this statement?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first night, the family was in the factory building. I was outside. And then the second night, all of us were outside. That's the only way it could be. No other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: There's a signature at the bottom of the statement. Can it be shown to the witness? Sir, can you see the signature?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it yours?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it right that in this statement you stated that you had spent the first night together with your family inside?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the first night. It was outside. I know that I was outside. I know that I slept outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau, what you have in these first two paragraphs there is what he has been basically testifying over an entire day yesterday and already about an hour this morning. So it's what I would call a supercondensation of -- so let's not be particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I'll move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you heard bombing when you were in Potocari, is this right?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the shells falling, yes. I heard that. Falling amidst the crowd in Potocari. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And can you remember that yesterday, on page 54 of yesterday's transcript, you stated, [In English] "Around the facility, around the people, around all the buildings, not just one building."?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These shells were landing on the people, around the crowd, all over the place, landing amid the buildings, in an area which perhaps covered one kilometre. That's how it usually was. Actually, they weren't landing in between the people, no. They were landing around the people, to ensure that the crowd stayed together, that people wouldn't disperse. That's what I heard and that's probably how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This shelling, did you hear it only during the first night or also during the second night?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it the first night, when they descended into Potocari. On the second night, I didn't hear it. I only heard individual shots and bursts of fire, and I could hear people moaning and screaming outside, which means that on the second night, they were taking people outside and firing at them from rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What you have just said, that they were shooting at people with rifles, you did not see it personally, is this right?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it, but you have to be crazy not to realise what's going on when people scream, moan, groan, and then all of a sudden the sounds stop. I didn't see it with my own eyes but you have to know, you must realise what had gone on then, and then later on they found mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, before Srebrenica fell, yesterday, on page 8 or rather 6 of the transcript, you said that humanitarian aid would sometimes arrive in Srebrenica. Do you know who was in charge of distributing humanitarian aid when it would come to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. I didn't inquire about that. I had this cow and I needed it for the milk, for my family, for grandchildren and so on, and there were some people who were distributing humanitarian aid when it arrived, yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know that part of this humanitarian aid was distributed to the army, to the ABiH, that was stationed in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I only know that it went to the warehouse. Now, as to whether there existed a separate warehouse for the military, I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know where the headquarters of the ABiH was in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either, because I didn't go to the headquarters. I wasn't supposed to go there. They didn't need me. I wasn't a soldier. As I told you, I looked after my cow. I made sure that it had enough food so that it would provide food for my grandchildren.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, your sons, were they not members of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One went to Zepa only to get food. He went there several times, to bring flour. He had four young children. So he wasn't involved. Many people didn't even have a rifle. They had no weapons. The other son did go sometimes. He went to dig trenches. They asked him to go and he would go, dig a trench and then come back home. So that in return, he would receive some flour, perhaps five kilograms of flour, for being involved. He did it for the food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, your answer is of course very informative but it doesn't really answer the question that was put to you. The question was a very direct one and that is whether -- it wasn't whether they did any work related to the military or the ABiH but whether they were members, members of the ABiH, whether they were enrolled in the ABiH, in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So forget that one went to Zepa and the other one went to dig trenches sometimes and got some flour in return but were either or both members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at any time before --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, now that you are asking it in this way, then I'll tell you that the younger one was involved, because if somebody attacks you, wouldn't you defend yourself? Everybody defends themselves when attacked. If you were to step on an ant, the ant would bite you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And what was his name, this younger son who was involved in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was killed. You have to know that. He was killed. He's gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sead Hasic, if you really want to know. He's dead. Are you interested in a dead man? They haven't found him yet. He isn't in any grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Hasic. Yes, Madam Fauveau, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Your son Hasic, Sead, was born in 1970, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Your other son, Hasic, Sadik, was he born in 1961?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not true. Who told you that? In 71? That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, who is the younger of the two?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found him and buried him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Who is the younger of the two, Sead or Sadik?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's entirely clear to you. Why are you asking me that, then? Sead is younger, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell me when your son Sadik was born?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have a problem of interpretation here. Because as I read the transcript, I'm soon coming to you, Ms. Soljan, when I read the transcript when it was put to him he was born in 61 he said no, that's not correct, then he said 71, that's true, which would make Sadik the younger of the two. Now he's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1971.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who was born in 1971?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1971, nobody was born.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wanted to make an objection to the relevance of this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the line of questioning he -- previously he said the younger of the two was a member of the army and the way it was going, it was obvious that Sead couldn't be the younger of the two. It would have been the elder of the two. So this is this is why we allowed the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Ms. Soljan. Yes, Madam Fauveau, can we go to the next series of questions, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, could you allow for the possibility that Hasic Sadik, your other son, was also a member of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't. He never went into any combat. That's true. You can think what you want but he never went into any action. I know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Even in 1992, he wasn't a member then of the Armija?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could I submit a document we found last night to the witness? We found it in the database. It is a collection of documents that had not been disclosed to us. Unfortunately, we don't have the document in the system but of course I've got copies for the Chamber. I've already disclosed these to the Prosecution and I'd like to show it now to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what document is this? What does it intend to prove?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a list of members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Bosnianovici unit where we have the name of Sadik, son of Ahmo, born in 1961.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any objections to the actual showing of the list. However, again, I do object to the line of questioning. I don't see what the relevance is to the facts of his sons belonging to the ABiH or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Madam Fauveau. You have permission to show the witness the document. On the other hand, we would like to know, in line with the -- yes. Madam Fauveau, we are of course proceeding with this showing of this document to the witness. On the other hand, in line with the objection made by Ms. Soljan, it's important for us to know what is the relevance of proving that one of his sons or both of his sons were members of the armed forces of the -- of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I would gladly explain this to you. I don't know whether it's good to do so in the presence of the witness or with him absent. The answer is very simple and I would not like to hurt him unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have the witness answer the question first and then you explain the relevance, Madam Fauveau. Yes, Mr. Hasic, you are being shown a list.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, on page 2 of the document, 02115729, that's the number of that page, second page, please, the last name under number 41, we can read, "Hasic, son of Ahmo, Sadik, born in 1961." Is this your son, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the source of this document, Madam Fauveau? I know it has been -- you found it in the --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, unfortunately, I have no information apart from the fact that I found it in the EDS database. It is a document that comes from the Prosecution, that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps the Prosecution tomorrow or later on will indicate to us the provenance of this document. Do you intend to tender this or not, or is it going to remain one of the documents that have been --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, yes. I'd rather have it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, perhaps you can tell us what the relevance of this series of questions is, the fact that he may have had one or more sons enrolled in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is merely with regard to the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is the case, I don't think you have got that far, Ms. Fauveau, but let's go to the next series of questions. This one will become -- we need to know what Exhibit number it's going to have. Just mark it for me, that's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you stated that your son would every now and then go to Zepa. Does this mean that the residents of Srebrenica could go to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could have, but many of them perished in the trip. They were carrying 30 to 40 kilograms on their back. It would be a trip lasting 11 hours, but they had to go. Many of them perished. They never made it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it right to say that when the UNPROFOR withdrew from Jadar in July 1995, they left a large quantity of fuel behind?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from others that a large quantity of fuel stayed or was left in a cistern. I don't know whether this was left on purpose or whether it was confiscated, captured. I can't say anything about that. I heard that from others. I didn't see anything. Yes. They did withdraw from Jadar. They came to Srebrenica. And then they surrendered there and pulled back.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, you stated, on page 49 of the transcript, that the departure took five days for people to leave, to go to Potocari. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that it took five days for people to leave Potocari. I did say that. Four to five days before -- I mean it wasn't possible to leave in less than four to five days. I left on Thursday but there were a lot of people left still after I left. Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, I left and then there were people still left on Friday. I don't know if they all left on Friday. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, why do you speak about things you're not familiar with, you don't know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. Don't answer that question. Don't answer. Ms. Fauveau, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you so much, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Krgovic will be putting questions to you now on behalf of General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Hasic. My colleagues for the most part covered the topics that I wanted to ask the witness about so I will only have a couple of short questions for this witness. Mr. Hasic, yesterday when you testified, you described an incident that took place when you left Bratunac and when you were in the buses going to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember mentioning a man who was fleeing and who was fired at?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's possible that this happened already at the entrance to Pilica. I don't know exactly. There was a school on the right side and that's where this happened. There was another school. We continued on, and where we turned, this was the school that was on the left-hand side, and that's where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood your testimony yesterday, you saw when that man fled but you didn't see the moment when he was actually hit. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him through the woods and I saw him being cut down with two bursts of gunfire. The first one didn't get him but the second one did and he fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember testifying in the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This was in July 2003. I'm now going to read a part of your testimony from that case. It's transcript of the 14th of July 2003, page 1190. Line 11. I'm going to read this in English and you are going to receive a translation in the language that you understand. [In English] "I heard the bursts of fire but someone else told me that they had killed him, but I didn't see the victim fall. I was told that he had been killed." [Interpretation] What I have just read, does that correspond to what you saw at the time?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It corresponds like this and like that. The main point is that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't see that?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it, but I saw it through the woods. I mean, I didn't see him personally, but I saw it in the -- in the woods, and I know that there were two bursts of gunfire. The first one didn't hit him, the second one cut him down, then they said he fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But this is something that other people told you?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those who were right there, standing in front of the bus. They said -- I was in front of the door, to the bus. He was killed. That's the point. Doesn't matter if I saw it or didn't see it. He lost his life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So you assume he was killed?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed for sure. I do not assume it. He was definitely killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Krgovic. Yes, finally, we come to the last set of cross-examinations, and it's Mr. Sarapa, I take it, who will be conducting the cross-examination, Mr. Haynes? Yes, Mr. Sarapa is appearing for accused Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have 15 minutes to the break, so it would be appreciated if you could manage to finish within those 15 minutes. If not, of course, you will have the time that you require.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, yesterday you said the following in your testimony. For the purposes of interpretation, this is page 7, lines 4 to 6. "July for five days straight actually, shelling of Srebrenica, around Srebrenica, so on the 11th of July we wanted to get to the UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] Do you stand by what was said?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a question in relation to this, in view of this shelling. Did you see dead and wounded people on the streets of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw when a shell fell just beneath my house, a bit lower, just a bit down from my house, when a shell fell, and one woman and a child were wounded there. They were taken away from there. Then also in other places, how would it be possible with shells falling amongst the people that people are not wounded?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: How many dead and wounded people did you see, if you say that shells were falling in the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see many.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No thank you. I want to say the following. I wasn't free to walk around the town of Srebrenica and to remove the wounded and the injured and to help them, when I could have been hit by a shell too. I was in a room. I was just listening and watching and following where shells were falling. I was in a shelter. I wasn't free to move around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I would like to move to my next question. In response to Ms. Fauveau's question regarding fuel, you said how you found out about this. But there is your statement of the 6th of July 1996, which was given to the Tuzla commission for gathering information about war crimes, and in that statement, you state the following. This is our document 7D00014. In the English translation, this is on page 2, paragraph 6. I'm going to read it. [In English] "I know that when the UNPROFOR members withdraw, especially from Jadar, large quantities of fuel and other equipment remained behind them and that this was taken and used by the Chetniks." [Interpretation] You answered the question about fuel to Ms. Fauveau but I would like to know how you got this information about the equipment that was left behind.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this from others up there. Perhaps soldiers who were guarding or who were on guard duty in trenches, that the UNPROFOR had withdrawn and that a quantity of fuel had stayed in Jadar. I don't know how it was captured or how it stayed. It's not clear to me but mostly this is what other people said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: You're talking about fuel again but I'm actually asking you about equipment?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what other equipment was there. I didn't say that any other equipment had stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I would like to have the witness look at his statement of the 6th of July. This is page 2, paragraph 5, where it is said, during the withdrawal -- during the withdrawal of the UNPROFOR, especially from Jadar, I know that there was a large quantity of fuel and other equipment that was left behind. So I would like to know about the equipment, since the witness has already answered the question about fuel.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying anything about equipment. I know I talked about the fuel. I heard about the fuel from others. I didn't see it but I don't recall saying anything about equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I would like the witness to look at the statement he provided on the 6th of July 1996, page 2, and we can also look at his signature at the end of page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is already been read in both English and B/C/S to the witness. I don't think it's really necessary for him to be going through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it the same document that was shown to him before?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: It is not the same document that was shown to him before but what I was saying was that the honourable counsel has just read the passages both in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but he wants to show him the relevant part in the document itself and his signature. I think that's -- we can allow that. In other words, he's being shown visually where he's supposed to have stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the witness has just replied that he never talked about equipment but here on page 2 it says and I read it out that during the withdrawal of UNPROFOR and I don't have to repeat that, a large quantity of fuel and other equipment remained behind. So the equipment is mentioned and this is why I'm referring back then to his signature at the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know about the fuel and I know today that this was said, but I don't remember mentioning any equipment. I really don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it we can safely move forward because at the end of the day this is happening in this Tribunal every day. We get statements that are translated and brought forward which do not necessarily always reflect 100 per cent what the prospective witness or interviewee would have actually stated. So at the end of the day, where is it going to get you, Mr. Sarapa? I mean, you can show him -- you can of course show him his signature. He will tell you, yes, that's my signature. But he's still maintaining that it's what he's stating now that is correct and what -- and not what is contained in that statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps something is written down by mistake. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Very well. I would like to ask you something about your surrender now. Yesterday, you said the following. I'm going to read a part of what you said. This is on page 43, lines 19 to 21. [In English] "We went down to the road. There was a bus with two policemen there and the driver." [Interpretation] First, a question in relation to the bus. Was it a military bus or a civilian bus?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's possible that it was a civilian bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you remember if the bus had any markings?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know. If it was a military bus, I think that it would have been a multi-coloured bus just like the uniforms that they wore, but I recall that it was a kind of whitish colour. I would think that it was a civilian bus then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. And the policemen, were they military policemen or civilian policemen?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seemed to me -- I don't know. As far as I can recall, they were wearing blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Are you sure that they were blue or are you just maybe remembering it like that?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Yesterday, you testified that -- I'm going to read. It's on page 32, lines 11 and 12. [In English] "I was not looking out for insignia. I just noticed their variegated uniforms." [Interpretation] I think that they had uniforms. I'm going to ask a question about this. Since you didn't pay attention to ranks and insignia, does that mean that you couldn't really tell right there who was a soldier and who was an officer?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is something that I don't remember. I don't remember what sort of uniforms they wore. All I recall was that they were policemen and there was a driver. They were going from house to house, as if they were on mobilisation duty, as if they were looking for people, they were looking for people by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to point out that this reference on page 32, lines 11 and 12 this is not referring to the very same incident. It is the incident -- this is the bussing from Bratunac that this is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sarapa, I can't confirm or deny that because I don't have that in front of me here, but if that is the case, I think you need to readdress the whole matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am speaking about the incident in front of the school in Pilica.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in front of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Were you able to tell who was an officer and who was a regular soldier, since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because this last thing I want to do is to have the witness confused. Let me go one page up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, please. Now, page 32, line 21, this is how it all started: "I would like to ask you something about your surrender now." Yesterday you said the following: I'm going to read part of, this is page 42, lines 19, 21 in English. "We went down to the road. There was a bus with two policemen there and the driver." First a question in relation to the bus and then you continue. So we are -- you introduced your series of questions in relation to his surrender. To my knowledge, he surrendered only once. He surrendered only once. And that was after his miraculous escape from death. In Potocari he did not surrender. He was just captured. In Bratunac, he was in a state of let's call it detention. In Pilica, he was still in a state of detention. So I just don't want the witness to get confused. Please be specific. You seem to be alleging that this incident that he referred to refers to one site. He is stating it's another site. And I just wondering in my mind whether either of the two refer to his surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I believe -- I just want to correct what I said earlier. The most recent citing to page 32, line 11, dealt with the Pilica bussing, so the bussing from Pilica. What Mr. Sarapa had started talking about initially was about the surrender and the buses at the surrender spot after, as you said, the miraculous escape from death of Mr. Hasic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a break now, Mr. Sarapa, and you'll take this up immediately after. We'll have a 25-minute break. The important thing is that the witness is put in the -- in the right direction before being asked to answer any question. Thank you, we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: May I start?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to clarify the question for the sake of the witness. I'm now referring to Pilica, to Pilica events before his surrender. The questions follow a topic, not a chronology. The previous question pertained to surrender, but the questions dealt with the insignia worn by those who were present. Now I have an identical question but in relation to a different event. To be more specific, the events in Pilica. Can you please look at page 31, line 19. The Bench put a question -- rather, not to the witness, but rather to my learned friend from the Prosecution, that this centred on the events in Pilica, and this can be gleaned from page 32, where in line 11 and 12, it says, "I wasn't looking for insignia. I just noticed [In English] uniforms." [Interpretation] My question is: Could the witness tell who was a soldier, who was an officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could tell, if I saw insignia. But I wasn't interested in that a great deal, and I could see that the soldiers were coming and then when the order came to tie us, it could have been that there were two officers who were there and who issued that order and who said, "These people need to be tied up."

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No further questions concerning this subject. I would now like to turn to a different topic. Namely, Karakaj. Yesterday's transcript page 47, lines 12 to 14, I would quote, "On of our people said, 'It's a good thing the Red Cross is here. They will be accompanying us.' So that's how we set off and we were being escorted by the Red Cross."

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question to you: Did you see the Red Cross representatives in Karakaj or did you hear from others that they were there?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then when we came to Batkovici, the Red Cross was there awaiting us and registered us, and they told us at that point that there had been no registration up to that time. There was a camp there and the war was going on but nobody was registered up until that date which was the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I would like now to turn to a different topic, namely transportation from Karakaj to Batkovici. Page 47 of yesterday's transcript, line 5 to 7. [In English] "I went to the truck and then I could see that inside there were some other people who had been caught in the woods. There were 27 of them altogether. And the two of us also, 29."

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to put a question to you in relation to this. There were 29 of you on the truck. Did you talk to other people about the events that preceded what was going on at that point and why you were taken there?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't discuss anything there. We just heard that they had been captured somewhere and had spent the night in Karakaj and then on that day --

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Didn't they tell you about the locations where they had been captured or where they surrendered?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were captured in the vicinity of Zvornik, in the woods in that area, but I don't know the specific name of that forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to turn to a different topic, namely the corpses that were allegedly seen on the truck. This transpired after the witness managed to save himself but before he surrendered. There is a statement that was recorded by the commission for investigation and documentation in Tuzla on the 20th of March 1996. This is our document 7D00012. On page 2, in paragraph 2, it says, "The five of us set out further, but soon after that, I found myself alone because I couldn't keep up with them. I came to a road leading to Karakaj, Zvornik municipality, where I saw traces of blood," and then this is the important bit. "At that point in time a truck was approaching me. As I was unable to turn I passed next to it. But with the corner of my eye, I noticed that there were corpses on the truck and the truck turned from that road to a minor road leading towards the forest."

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: That's correct. All right. There is also a statement that the witness gave to Mr. Ruez, the investigator. This was on the 25th of May 1996, where on page 5, paragraph 2, it says, "[In English] I don't know how far I was from the execution field. A road came from the left and I saw a truck arriving from the nearby intersection and had no time to hide. I just continued to walk along the road towards the intersection and when the truck passed by, I turned my head and saw that the rear of the truck was loaded with a pile of dead bodies." [Interpretation] Is this correct as well?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same thing. One and the other are the same or similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I'd like to clarify just one point. Did you turn your head or not to follow the truck in order to see what was on the truck? Because in your 25th of May statement you say, "I turned my head" whereas in your 20th of March statement, you say that you saw it with the corner of your eye.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the truck drew close --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. Move to the next question, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: In your 6th of July statement, 6th of July 1996, page 6 it says, "On this occasion I would like to point out that while travelling from Pilica through the meadows and forest, I saw in many locations corpses of dead civilians, and I can show all these locations from Pilica where the executions were conducted to the locations where I saw the bodies, if somebody requires this information." I'd like to ask you this: In how many locations did you see these corpses, if you can remember? Can you answer this question?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw in one stream, where I was hiding myself, I saw many bones in the stream. I drank water from this stream. I was so thirsty that I disregarded the fact that there were bones there, and I saw that these were human bones and I saw this in one location. I don't know when these people were killed, but there were just bones there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could we clarify something? In your statement, it says that you saw corpses of dead civilians in a number of locations and now you're mentioning bones. So which is true?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that I saw corpses in many locations. That's not true. Now, as to whether I stated that, I don't think so, because I normally don't say things that I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could we now show 7D00014, page 6, to the witness? Paragraph 4. Or rather paragraph 6. Once again, I'd like the witness to read this out. This sentence which begins with, "On this occasion, I'd like to point out."

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read that because it's too small. As for the corpses that I saw, I saw them, but when they brought us to the execution site, as I was leaving the bus, when they were directing us to our death site. Along that path, leading to the execution site, there were corpses there, yes. These people were killed there and they remained lying on that path. This is what I saw and this is what I spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No. This involves something else, as you were travelling from Pilica through meadows and forests.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true and I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Very well. Then I will turn to a different question. Regarding that incident when 12 young men aged between 15 and 16 were taken out, the witness said on several occasions, he gave his testimony about that. However, in your statement, on the 20th of March 1996, the witness said as follows: "On the same day, they took out 12 young men between 15 and 16 years of age, saying that they were taking them to the front of Fikret Abdic in Krajina. Following that, they took out several people aged up to 30 years." This is document 7D00012. Document 7D00014, when speaking of this same event, and this was dated on the 6th of July 1996, the witness mentions only 12 young men between 15 and 16 years, describing the incident almost identically, but fails to mention the seven other men, older ones, up to 30 years. So I'd like to ask the witness whether this means -- or, rather, what are the reasons why, in his second statement, he did not mention the other seven people who were older. Were they really taken out or not?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said about the young men that they wanted to send to Fikret Abdic, they were lined up and taken out. What happened to them, I don't know. As for the other seven who were up to 30 years old, I said that they were perhaps taken out during my stay there. They were taken out from my room, these people, and then they were outside, moaning and screaming. I didn't say that they were taken all out at the same time. I said in the course of my stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Further on in your statement -- can we go into private session? Or closed session? Because this is a question dealing with something that might reveal the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go into private session for awhile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Our document 7D00012, which is a statement dated the 20th of March 1996, at the end of the statement, there is a sketch attached and I would like to put a few brief questions to the witness about the sketch. Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, are we going to see this sketch or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could that be shown to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, what is written on this sketch, is it in your handwriting or not, or rather, who wrote this down?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see my handwriting anywhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you to look at the bottom right corner where it says, "20th of March 1996." And then below it, there is a signature, illegible to me. I'd like to ask you: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it you don't have any further questions, Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No, I don't have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there re-examination, Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Just a few very brief questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, just taking you back to the day you were bused to the building in Pilica. Do you recall where the buses went as they were taking you to this building in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were passing through Bratunac, through Konjevic Polje, Drinjaca, Zvornik, crossed over a bridge into Serbia and then we were travelling through Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He gave a full description of the route taken when he first started giving evidence. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I'll ask it a little more exactly, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: From the moment you stopped in Pilica, do you recall where your bus went? Or more precisely, from the incident where a man, dead man, had been taken out from the bus and another man had been shot at, do you recall where the buses went from that point?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was going ahead, in the direction where it was intending to go, towards Pilica. And it was perhaps shortly before entering into Pilica, there was this building on the right side and then it continued in the same direction. It didn't cover too much ground and then it turned left, to this school. That's why I was saying that I wasn't sure whether it was a school or a cultural hall. It's a one storey building with a ground floor and one storey more but I really didn't pay attention exactly to what it was. I was afraid. You just kept your head down and you didn't look from side to side. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: No more questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Soljan. Mr. Hasic, we have finished with your testimony, which means that you are free to go back home as soon as our staff finalise the travel arrangements for you. I can assure you that you will receive all the assistance you will receive all the.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will receive all the assistance you require between now and your return. I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence. I thank you on my own behalf, on behalf of Judge Prost, Judge Stole, but also on behalf of Judge Kwon, who is not with us today. And on behalf of everyone, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to thank you because you invited me to tell the real truth and what is just and I would like to thank Del Ponte whose intention is to catch the criminals and to carry out justice, to administer justice. I would also like to thank everyone and I wish you fortunate and successful work. Doesn't matter who the criminals are, whether they are like this or like that, who they are. What's important is if they did commit a crime, they should be brought to trial and they should bear the consequences of their acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I thank you so much, Mr. Hasic. You will now be escorted by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, while the witness is being ushered out of the courtroom, yesterday Mr. Bourgon raised a procedural matter relating to the next witness, and I said that at the time that I did not anticipate great problems. Have you in the meantime met, Mr. McCloskey, and tried to clarify the matter further?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We did see each other briefly. I think it's just a -- I don't think it's a big issue any further. I know he would have preferred for each of the exhibits to have 65 ter numbers. As I stated, they either are identical or very similar to and so we didn't do that. We will endeavour to do that in the future, especially when we get of course to military documents and intercepts. This will absolutely happen. But I've also asked him if there is any documents they feel surprised by or they feel new to tell me and I would consider pulling them. No one has said anything and I don't believe there are any such photographs to that effect so I don't see Mr. Bourgon here, but I think we probably would take the same positions we took yesterday, and I know Ms. Nikolic would like to address us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In particular, before I give you the floor, Ms. Nikolic, in particular, the only concern that I have, having gone through this, is you indicate as a Prosecution exhibit a CD containing 271 images, namely crime scenes and maps, with P reference number as P02103. And that would be the intended exhibit number, as I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to get into the -- our -- what we had planned and how we had planned to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me not -- okay. Let's deal with it as we go along. Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.
